claim_set.claim: Popularity has significant consequences for psychological development in children, influencing their self-esteem, social skills, and overall well-being.

claim_set.claim: Children who are consistently popular tend to experience higher levels of self-esteem and confidence, while those who are rejected or ostracized may struggle with low self-esteem and depression.
claim_set.source: Children who are consistently popular tend to experience higher levels of self-esteem and confidence (Hartup & Stevens, 1997). Conversely, children who are rejected or ostracized by their peers may struggle with low self-esteem and depression (Bukatko & Daehler, 2003).

claim_set.claim: An overemphasis on popularity can lead to negative social dynamics within schools, including bullying and social marginalization, and can have long-term consequences for psychological development.
claim_set.source: Moreover, research has highlighted the potential risks associated with excessive popularity during childhood. Children who are popular often occupy positions of power and influence within their social networks, which can lead to bullying, exclusion, and social marginalization of those who are less popular (Cillessen & Mayeux, 2004). Moreover, the pressure to conform to certain social norms or expectations can result in a homogenized social climate, stifling creativity, individuality, and diversity (Hartup & Stevens, 1997).

While sympathy may be motivated by a desire for personal connection or understanding, it cannot be reduced to mere self-love. Moral sentiments encompass both personal virtues and social norms, as well as the capacity for individuals to recognize their own fallibility and limitations (Smith 1964, p. 134).
